title: Atomic Structure

toc.title: 2.1 Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models; the spectrum of hydrogen
2.2 de Broglie's equation and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
2.3 Orbitals and quantum numbers; Aufbau, Pauli and Hund; electronic configuration

html:
Atomic structure carries about two questions in the paper.

They are among the most predictable in Physical Chemistry: a Bohr-model number (radius, speed or energy, almost always as a ratio in n and Z), a hydrogen-spectrum question (series, wavelength, number of lines), a de Broglie or uncertainty calculation, or a quantum-number rule (which set is allowed, how many nodes, the configuration of Cr, Cu or a transition-metal ion).

Learn the proportionalities and most questions take under a minute.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Rutherford's α-scattering conclusions, and why the model fails (stability, line spectra).
  • Bohr: mvr = nh/2\pi; r \propto n^2/Z (0.529 Å), v \propto Z/n (2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹), E \propto -Z^2/n^2 (−13.6 eV); KE = −E, PE = 2E.
  • Hydrogen spectrum: 1/\lambda = R_H Z^2 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2); the five series and their regions; number of lines n(n-1)/2.
  • de Broglie \lambda = h/mv = h/p; Heisenberg \Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi.
  • The four quantum numbers and their allowed values; radial nodes n - l - 1, angular nodes l.
  • Aufbau (n + l rule), Pauli and Hund; the Cr and Cu exceptions; ions lose 4s electrons before 3d; counting unpaired electrons.

2.1 Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models; the spectrum of hydrogen

Rutherford's nuclear model (1911)

Rutherford (with Geiger and Marsden) fired a beam of α-particles (He²⁺ nuclei) at a very thin gold foil and counted the flashes they made on a zinc sulphide screen placed all around it.

Observation Conclusion
Most α-particles passed straight through Most of the atom is empty space
A few were deflected through large angles The positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region — the nucleus — that repels the α-particles
A very small fraction bounced straight back The nucleus is extremely small and holds almost all the mass

The model: a tiny, dense, positive nucleus (radius about 10⁻¹⁵ m) with electrons revolving round it in circular paths like planets (atom radius about 10⁻¹⁰ m — about 10⁵ times larger). Electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force.

Why it failed. (1)

Stability by classical electromagnetic theory an accelerating (revolving) charge radiates energy, so the electron should spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a microsecond — atoms would collapse. (2)

Spectra a spiralling electron would give a continuous spectrum, but atoms give line spectra. (3) It says nothing about how the electrons are arranged.

Bohr's model (1913)

  1. Electrons revolve only in certain permitted circular orbits — stationary states — in which they do not radiate energy.
  2. Only those orbits are allowed in which the angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h/2\pi: mvr = nh/2\pi, n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
  3. Energy is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits, as one photon: \Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = h\nu.

For a one-electron species with nuclear charge Z (H, He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺) these give:

Quantity Formula Hydrogen, n = 1 Varies as
Radius r_n = 0.529\,n^2/Z Å 0.529 Å (Bohr radius) n^2/Z
Speed v_n = 2.18\times10^{6}\,Z/n m s⁻¹ 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ Z/n
Total energy E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2 eV −13.6 eV = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J Z^2/n^2
Kinetic energy KE = -E_n +13.6 eV Z^2/n^2
Potential energy PE = 2E_n −27.2 eV Z^2/n^2
Angular momentum nh/2\pi h/2\pi n
Time for one revolution 2\pi r/v 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁶ s n^3/Z^2

Hydrogen levels: E₁ = −13.6, E₂ = −3.40, E₃ = −1.51, E₄ = −0.85, E∞ = 0 eV. The energy is negative because the electron is bound; zero means a free electron at rest at infinity.

As n increases the energy rises (becomes less negative) and the gaps between levels shrink. Ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 Z² eV: H 13.6 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹), He⁺ 54.4 eV, Li²⁺ 122.4 eV.

Comparing orbits with ratios

Problem. Compare the radius, speed and energy of the electron in the n = 2 orbit of He⁺ with those in the n = 1 orbit of hydrogen.

Solution. He⁺: Z = 2, n = 2. Radius ∝ n²/Z = 4/2 = 2, so r = 2 × 0.529 = 1.058 Å (twice hydrogen's). Speed ∝ Z/n = 1, so it is the same, 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Energy ∝ Z²/n² = 4/4 = 1, so it is the same, −13.6 eV. No formula beyond the ratios is needed.

Defect of Bohr's model What it could not explain
Many-electron atoms Works only for one-electron species; fails even for He
Fine structure Each line, at high resolution, is a group of close lines
Zeeman and Stark effects Splitting of lines in magnetic and electric fields
Dual nature and uncertainty Treats the electron as a particle on a definite path, which de Broglie and Heisenberg forbid
Molecules Cannot explain chemical bonding or molecular shapes

The spectrum of hydrogen

Light comes in packets (photons) of energy E = h\nu = hc/\lambda (Planck). The wavenumber \bar{\nu} = 1/\lambda is the number of waves per unit length. A useful shortcut: E (eV) = 1240/λ (nm).

When hydrogen at low pressure is excited in a discharge tube, its light, passed through a prism, gives sharp bright lines on a dark background: an emission line spectrum.

Light passed through cool hydrogen shows dark lines at the same wavelengths: an absorption spectrum. Hot solids give continuous spectra, atoms give line spectra and molecules give band spectra.

Every hydrogen line fits the Rydberg equation, which Bohr's model derives:

\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda} = R_H Z^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \qquad n_2 > n_1

with R_H = 1.097\times10^{7} m⁻¹ (109 678 cm⁻¹); Z = 1 for hydrogen.

Series n₁ n₂ Region First (longest) line Series limit (shortest)
Lyman 1 2, 3, 4 … ultraviolet ≈ 122 nm 91.2 nm
Balmer 2 3, 4, 5 … visible 656 nm (Hα, red) 365 nm
Paschen 3 4, 5, 6 … near infrared 1875 nm 820 nm
Brackett 4 5, 6, 7 … infrared 4051 nm 1458 nm
Pfund 5 6, 7, 8 … far infrared 7458 nm 2279 nm

The four visible Balmer lines are Hα 656 nm (red), Hβ 486 nm (blue-green), Hγ 434 nm (blue-violet) and Hδ 410 nm (violet). Within a series the lines crowd together towards the series limit (n_2 = \infty).

How many lines? When electrons in a sample of atoms fall from level n₂ to level n₁ by every possible route, the number of distinct lines is \Delta n(\Delta n + 1)/2 with \Delta n = n_2 - n_1; from level n to the ground state this is n(n-1)/2.

A single atom can give at most n_2 - n_1 lines on one trip down.

A Balmer wavelength two ways

Problem. Find the wavelength of the line emitted in the jump n = 4 → n = 2 in hydrogen.

Solution. Rydberg: 1/\lambda = 1.097\times10^{7}(1/4 - 1/16) = 1.097\times10^{7}\times0.1875 = 2.06\times10^{6} m⁻¹, so λ = 4.86 × 10⁻⁷ m = 486 nm (Hβ, blue-green). Energy route: ΔE = 3.40 − 0.85 = 2.55 eV, and λ = 1240/2.55 = 486 nm.

Counting spectral lines

Problem. Electrons in a sample of hydrogen atoms are excited to n = 6. How many lines can appear in the emission spectrum, and how many of them belong to the Balmer series?

Solution. All lines: 6 × 5/2 = 15. Balmer lines end on n = 2 and can start from n = 3, 4, 5 or 6: 4 lines.

The traps in spectrum questions
  • The first line of a series is its longest wavelength (smallest energy gap, n_2 = n_1 + 1); the series limit (n_2 = \infty) is its shortest.
  • For He⁺ or Li²⁺ multiply the wavenumber by Z² — not by Z.
  • Wavelength is inversely proportional to (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2): a ratio of wavelengths is the inverse ratio of these brackets. First Lyman : first Balmer = (5/36) : (3/4) = 5 : 27.

2.2 de Broglie's equation and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle

de Broglie's wave–particle duality (1924)

Light behaves both as a wave (diffraction) and as particles (photoelectric effect). de Broglie proposed that every moving particle also has a wave associated with it:

\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m\,KE}}

For an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of V volts, KE = eV, so λ ≈ 12.27/√V Å. Because λ ∝ 1/m, the wave is noticeable only for microscopic particles.

Davisson and Germer (1927) confirmed it by diffracting electrons from a nickel crystal; the electron microscope uses the same idea.

Bohr's rule from waves. A stable orbit must hold a whole number of electron waves: 2\pi r = n\lambda = nh/mv, which rearranges to mvr = nh/2\pi — Bohr's postulate.

Electron against cricket ball

Problem. Find the de Broglie wavelength of (i) a 0.15 kg cricket ball bowled at 40 m s⁻¹, (ii) an electron moving at 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).

Solution. (i) λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.15 × 40) = 1.1 × 10⁻³⁴ m — hopelessly small to detect. (ii) λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.18 × 10⁶) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the size of an atom — in fact equal to the circumference of the first Bohr orbit, 2π × 0.529 Å = 3.3 Å.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927)

Uncertainty principle

It is impossible to determine simultaneously, with complete accuracy, both the position and the momentum (or velocity) of a microscopic particle such as an electron: \Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq h/4\pi, that is \Delta x \cdot \Delta v \geq h/4\pi m.

The more exactly the position is fixed, the less exactly the momentum is known (and vice versa); if \Delta x = 0 then \Delta p would be infinite. A similar relation holds for energy and time, \Delta E \cdot \Delta t \geq h/4\pi.

The uncertainty is not a fault of instruments — observing an electron needs a photon, which disturbs it.

Consequence: a definite orbit (exact radius and exact speed together) has no meaning, so we speak only of the probability of finding an electron, i.e. of orbitals.

Uncertainty for an electron and a bullet

Problem. Find the minimum uncertainty in velocity of (i) an electron confined within 1.0 nm, (ii) a 10 g bullet whose position is known to within 1 μm. (m_e = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

Solution. Δv = h/(4π m Δx). (i) 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 5.8 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ — large. (ii) 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(4π × 0.010 × 1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.3 × 10⁻²⁷ m s⁻¹ — utterly negligible.

Where the factor goes wrong

The bound is h/4\pi, not h and not h/2\pi — setters put all three values among the options. And the principle is about simultaneous measurement: position alone, or momentum alone, can be measured as precisely as you like.

2.3 Orbitals and quantum numbers; Aufbau, Pauli and Hund; electronic configuration

Orbit and orbital

Orbit (Bohr) Orbital (quantum mechanics)
a definite circular path round the nucleus a three-dimensional region where the probability of finding the electron is maximum
two-dimensional, fixed radius three-dimensional, with a shape (s, p, d, f)
violates the uncertainty principle consistent with it
holds up to 2n² electrons holds at most 2 electrons

The four quantum numbers

Quantum number Symbol Allowed values Tells us
Principal n 1, 2, 3, … (K, L, M, N …) shell; size and main energy
Azimuthal (angular momentum) l 0 to (n − 1); 0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d, 3 = f subshell and shape
Magnetic m (mₗ) −l … 0 … +l, i.e. 2l + 1 values orientation in space
Spin s (mₛ) +½ or −½ direction of spin
Counting rule Formula Examples
Subshells in shell n n n = 3: 3s, 3p, 3d
Orbitals in a subshell 2l + 1 s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7
Electrons in a subshell 2(2l + 1) s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14
Orbitals in shell n n² n = 3: 9
Electrons in shell n 2n² n = 3: 18
Radial (spherical) nodes n − l − 1 3s: 2; 3p: 1; 3d: 0; 4d: 1
Angular nodes (nodal planes) l s 0, p 1, d 2
Total nodes n − 1 4f: 3
Orbital angular momentum √(l(l + 1)) · h/2π s: 0; p: √2 · h/2π

Subshells that do not exist — 1p, 2d and 3f — are favourite distractors: l must always be less than n.

Filling the orbitals: three rules

Aufbau, Pauli and Hund

Aufbau principle. In the ground state electrons occupy orbitals in order of increasing energy. The order follows the (n + l) rule: the lower n + l fills first; if two subshells have equal n + l, the one with lower n fills first.

Pauli's exclusion principle. No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers — so an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.

Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity. Electrons do not pair in degenerate orbitals (for example the three 2p) until each has one electron; the single electrons have parallel spins.

Electronic configurations, exceptions and ions

Species Configuration Unpaired e⁻
N (7) 1s² 2s² 2p³ 3
O (8) 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ 2
K (19) [Ar] 4s¹ 1
Sc (21) [Ar] 3d¹ 4s² 1
Cr (24) [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (not 3d⁴ 4s²) 6
Mn (25) [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s² 5
Fe (26) [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² 4
Cu (29) [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (not 3d⁹ 4s²) 1
Zn (30) [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 0
Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺ [Ar] 3d⁶ / [Ar] 3d⁵ 4 / 5
Cu⁺ / Cu²⁺ [Ar] 3d¹⁰ / [Ar] 3d⁹ 0 / 1
Mn²⁺ / Cr³⁺ / Zn²⁺ [Ar] 3d⁵ / [Ar] 3d³ / [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 5 / 3 / 0
  • Exceptions: Cr and Cu (also Mo 4d⁵ 5s¹, Ag 4d¹⁰ 5s¹, Au 5d¹⁰ 6s¹) take one 4s (ns) electron into the d subshell because half-filled (d⁵) and completely filled (d¹⁰) subshells are extra stable (symmetry and greater exchange energy).
  • Ions: electrons are removed first from the shell of highest n — 4s before 3d, although 4s filled first. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². Fe³⁺ (d⁵) is more stable than Fe²⁺ (d⁶), which is why iron(II) salts are slowly oxidised in air.
  • A species with unpaired electrons is paramagnetic (attracted by a magnet); with all electrons paired it is diamagnetic. Spin-only magnetic moment \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} BM for n unpaired electrons: Fe³⁺ (5) 5.92 BM, Cu²⁺ (1) 1.73 BM.
Configurations of iron and its ions

Problem. Write the configurations of Fe (Z = 26), Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ and give the number of unpaired electrons in each.

Solution. Fe: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². In the five 3d orbitals Hund's rule puts one electron in each and pairs the sixth: 4 unpaired. Fe²⁺: remove the two 4s electrons → [Ar] 3d⁶, 4 unpaired. Fe³⁺: remove one more from 3d → [Ar] 3d⁵, 5 unpaired (one in each d orbital).

Quantum-number checks in five seconds

"l below n, m within ±l, s only ±½." A set fails if l ≥ n (2, 2, …), if |m| > l (2, 1, −2, …) or if s is anything but ±½. Nodes: radial n − l − 1, angular l, total n − 1.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Formula / value
Bohr radius r_n = 0.529\,n^2/Z Å
Bohr speed v_n = 2.18\times10^{6}\,Z/n m s⁻¹
Bohr energy E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2 eV = -2.18\times10^{-18}\,Z^2/n^2 J = -1312\,Z^2/n^2 kJ mol⁻¹
KE and PE KE = −E; PE = 2E; PE/KE = −2
Angular momentum mvr = nh/2\pi
Photon E = h\nu = hc/\lambda; E (eV) = 1240/λ (nm); 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Rydberg 1/\lambda = R_H Z^2 (1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2), R_H = 1.097\times10^{7} m⁻¹
Number of lines \Delta n(\Delta n + 1)/2; to ground state n(n-1)/2
de Broglie \lambda = h/mv = h/p = h/\sqrt{2m\,KE}; electron through V volts: 12.27/√V Å
Heisenberg \Delta x\cdot\Delta p \geq h/4\pi; \Delta x\cdot\Delta v \geq h/4\pi m
Orbitals and electrons subshell 2l + 1 and 2(2l + 1); shell n² and 2n²
Nodes radial n − l − 1; angular l; total n − 1
Spin-only moment \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} BM

Ionisation energies: H 13.6 eV, He⁺ 54.4 eV, Li²⁺ 122.4 eV. Series: Lyman (n₁ = 1, UV), Balmer (2, visible), Paschen (3, IR), Brackett (4, IR), Pfund (5, far IR). Aufbau order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p 7s 5f 6d 7p. Exceptions: Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.

Chapter summary

  • Rutherford: most of the atom is empty; positive charge and mass sit in a nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ m across. The model fails on stability and on line spectra.
  • Bohr: stationary orbits with mvr = nh/2\pi; photons only on jumps, \Delta E = h\nu. For one-electron species r \propto n^2/Z, v \propto Z/n, E = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2 eV.
  • Hydrogen lines obey 1/\lambda = R_H(1/n_1^2 - 1/n_2^2): Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR). A sample falling from level n gives n(n-1)/2 lines.
  • de Broglie: \lambda = h/mv; significant only for tiny masses; 2\pi r = n\lambda gives Bohr's rule.
  • Heisenberg: \Delta x\cdot\Delta p \geq h/4\pi, so orbits give way to orbitals (probability regions).
  • Quantum numbers n, l (0 to n − 1), m (−l to +l), s (±½); radial nodes n − l − 1, angular nodes l.
  • Aufbau by (n + l), Pauli (two electrons per orbital, opposite spins), Hund (no pairing until each degenerate orbital has one). Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; ions lose 4s before 3d.

Practice questions

Set A — Recall (20 questions)

  9. de Broglie's equation for a particle of mass m moving with speed v isaλ = mv/hbλ = h/mvcλ = hv/mdλ = hm/v

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — Large-angle deflections and rebounds need a small, massive, positive centre: the nucleus. Fixed orbits (a) are Bohr's idea; wave behaviour (d) is de Broglie's.

2.(a) — An undeflected particle met nothing on its way, so most of the atom is empty space. Option(b) follows from the deflected particles, not the undeflected ones.

3. (d) — A revolving electron should radiate, spiral into the nucleus and give a continuous spectrum; the model explains(a) ,(b) and(c) .

4. (b) — Bohr's quantum condition mvr = nh/2π. The other forms are distortions of it.

5. (a) — E₁ = −13.6 eV; the negative sign shows a bound electron. −3.4 eV is the n = 2 level.

6. (c) — r₁ = 0.529 Å = 0.0529 nm. (a) has the right digits but the wrong unit; 2.116 Å is n = 2.

7. (d) — n₁ = 2: its first four lines (656, 486, 434, 410 nm) are visible. Lyman is ultraviolet; Paschen, Brackett and Pfund are infrared.

8. (b) — Lyman lines end on n = 1, Balmer on 2, Paschen on 3.

9. (b) — λ = h/mv = h/p: wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.

10. (c) — The product of the uncertainties can never be smaller than h/4π.

11. (a) — For an electron the uncertainty is comparable to atomic sizes and speeds; for heavy bodies it is immeasurably small.

12. (d) — 2n² (2, 8, 18, 32). n² is the number of orbitals; 2l + 1 counts orbitals in one subshell.

13. (c) — m runs from −2 to +2: −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, five values (five d orbitals).

14. (b) — l fixes the shape (s, p, d, f); n fixes size and energy, m the orientation, s the spin.

15. (d) — Pauli's principle; it limits an orbital to two electrons of opposite spin.

16.(a) — Degenerate orbitals are first singly occupied with parallel spins;(b) is Aufbau and(c) follows from Pauli.

17. (b) — Two lobes on opposite sides of a nodal plane; s is spherical and most d orbitals are cloverleaf-shaped.

18. (d) — The half-filled 3d⁵ subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron moves into 3d.

19. (c) — 4s has n + l = 4; 3d, 4p and 5s all have 5, and among them 3d has the lowest n.

20. (a) — n² = 9 orbitals (one 3s, three 3p, five 3d). 18 is the number of electrons.

Set B — Understanding (14 questions)

  8. The number of unpaired electrons in Fe³⁺ (Z = 26) isa3b5c4d6
  9. The electronic configuration of Cu²⁺ (Z = 29) isa[Ar] 3d⁹b[Ar] 3d⁸ 4s¹c[Ar] 3d¹⁰d[Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²
  10. In a many-electron atom, which of these subshells has the highest energy?a4sb3dc4pd5s
  11. The number of radial nodes in a 4d orbital isa0b2c1d3
  12. Writing nitrogen as 1s² 2s² 2pₓ² 2pᵧ¹, with 2p_z empty, violatesathe Aufbau principlebHund's rulecPauli's exclusion principledthe (n + l) rule
  13. Bohr's idea of a fixed circular orbit is rejected today mainly becauseait fixes position and momentum together, which uncertainty forbidsbelectrons have no masscthe nucleus is not positively chargeddhydrogen gives a continuous spectrum
  14. Bohr's quantum condition follows from de Broglie's idea if the circumference of an allowed orbit equalsaλ/nbnλ/2c2nλdnλ
Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — r ∝ n², so 1² : 2² : 3² = 1 : 4 : 9.

2. (d) — E ∝ −1/n², so the levels crowd together: 1→2 is 10.2 eV but 2→3 only 1.89 eV and 3→4 0.66 eV.

3. (a) — v = 2.18 × 10⁶ Z/n m s⁻¹: faster for a larger nuclear charge, slower in outer orbits. n²/Z is the radius dependence.

4. (c) — KE = −E = +3.4 eV and PE = 2E = −6.8 eV; check KE + PE = −3.4 eV.

5. (c) — λ = h/p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. With different masses their speeds and kinetic energies (p²/2m) differ.

6. (a) — For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1. The other sets obey l < n, |m| ≤ l and s = ±½.

7. (d) — n = 3 is the third shell and l = 1 is a p subshell: 3p.

8. (b) — Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵: one electron in each of the five d orbitals.

9. (a) — Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; remove the 4s electron, then one 3d electron: [Ar] 3d⁹.

Model answer D1: Bohr's model and the hydrogen spectrum (10 marks)

Introduction. Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom or line spectra.

Bohr (1913) proposed that an electron moves in fixed circular orbits (energy levels) without radiating, that its angular momentum is mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}, and that radiation is emitted or absorbed only when it jumps between orbits: \Delta E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}.

Results for hydrogen and hydrogen-like species (atomic number Z):

  1. Radius r_n = 52.9\,\dfrac{n^2}{Z}\ \text{pm}.
  2. Speed v_n = 2.19\times10^6\,\dfrac Zn\ \text{m s}^{-1}.
  3. Energy E_n = -13.6\,\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV} = -2.18\times10^{-18}\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{J}.
  4. Spectral lines: \bar\nu = \dfrac1\lambda = R_HZ^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right) with R_H = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}.
Series n_1 n_2 Region
Lyman 1 2, 3, ... ultraviolet
Balmer 2 3, 4, ... visible
Paschen 3 4, 5, ... infrared
Brackett 4 5, 6, ... infrared
Pfund 5 6, 7, ... far infrared

The number of lines for the jump from level n to the ground state, in all possible ways, is \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}.

Limitations. The model fails for atoms with more than one electron, cannot explain the splitting of lines in a magnetic field (Zeeman) or electric field (Stark), and contradicts the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi) and the dual nature of the electron (\lambda = h/mv).

Numerical.

  • The H_\alpha line (3 \to 2): \bar\nu = 1.097\times10^7\times\dfrac{5}{36} = 1.524\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}, so \lambda = 656\ \text{nm}.
  • Ionisation energy of He⁺ (Z = 2, n = 1) = 13.6\times4 = 54.4\ \text{eV}.
  • The n = 4 orbit of hydrogen has r = 16\times52.9 = 846\ \text{pm}, and a jump 4 \to 1 gives 13.6(1 - \tfrac1{16}) = 12.75\ \text{eV}.

Conclusion. Bohr's model explains the hydrogen spectrum through quantised energy levels but fails for many-electron atoms, which need the quantum mechanical model.

Model answer D2: quantum numbers and electronic configuration (10 marks)

Introduction. In the quantum mechanical model, the position of an electron is described by an orbital, a region of high probability, and four quantum numbers.

Quantum number Symbol Allowed values Tells
Principal n 1, 2, 3, \ldots shell, size and energy
Azimuthal l 0 to n - 1 subshell shape (s, p, d, f)
Magnetic m_l -l to +l orientation, giving 2l + 1 orbitals
Spin m_s +\tfrac12 or -\tfrac12 spin direction

A shell holds 2n^2 electrons and a subshell 2(2l + 1) electrons. The number of radial nodes is n - l - 1 and the angular nodes equal l.

Rules for filling.

  1. Aufbau principle: orbitals fill in the increasing order of (n + l), and for equal values the lower n first: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, ...
  2. Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom have all four quantum numbers the same, so an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin.
  3. Hund's rule: electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.

Exceptions. Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable (exchange energy, symmetry). So chromium is [\text{Ar}]3d^54s^1 (not 3d^44s^2) and copper is [\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1.

In forming cations, electrons leave the 4s before the 3d, for example Fe³⁺ is [\text{Ar}]3d^5.

Magnetic moment. \mu = \sqrt{n(n + 2)}\ \text{BM}, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. A substance with unpaired electrons is paramagnetic and one with none is diamagnetic.

Numerical. Fe³⁺ (3d^5) has n = 5, so \mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\ \text{BM}. Cu²⁺ (3d^9) has n = 1 and \mu = \sqrt3 = 1.73\ \text{BM}. Zn²⁺ (3d^{10}) has n = 0 and is diamagnetic. The valid sets for n = 3 give 2n^2 = 18 electrons in 9 orbitals.

Conclusion. Four quantum numbers fix every electron, and the Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules, with the special stability of half-filled and fully-filled subshells, give the configuration.
